title: Azure application works in one region but not another
description: Diagnose a regional failure where an Azure application serves users in East US but returns errors or timeouts for West Europe users, including routing, quota, and data-replication issues.

data.text: East US is healthy. West Europe returns 504s. The deployment succeeded, the database is online, and the application logs look normal—but users in Europe are hitting errors. The problem is not the code; it is the regional boundary. Azure resources are region-scoped unless explicitly deployed globally, and routing, data replication, and DNS all have regional failure modes that only appear when you serve traffic from a secondary location.

data.title: Core concepts
items: Azure resources are region-scoped unless explicitly deployed globally
Traffic Manager uses DNS-based routing; Front Door uses anycast with health probes
Geo-replication copies data to a secondary region but does not make it automatically writable
Regional quotas can block provisioning in a secondary region even when the primary succeeds
Private Endpoint DNS must resolve to the regional private IP, not the public endpoint

terms.definition: A set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected through a dedicated regional low-latency network.
Physically separate locations within an Azure region that protect applications and data from datacenter-level failures.
Copying data to a geographically distant Azure region to protect against regional outages and enable disaster recovery.
A DNS-based traffic load balancer that routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint across regions.

items: App Service or Function App was deployed only to the primary region
Azure Front Door or Traffic Manager profile is not routing to the secondary region
SQL Database or Cosmos DB does not have read replicas or geo-failover enabled
Storage account firewall or private endpoint restricts access by region
App Configuration or Key Vault references are region-specific and not replicated
CI/CD pipeline targets only one region or the secondary deployment failed silently

cards.title: Azure SQL Database
cards.description: Supports auto-failover groups and active geo-replication for cross-region high availability.

cards.title: Cosmos DB
cards.description: Offers multi-master and single-master with automatic failover across regions.

cards.title: App Service
cards.description: Region-scoped compute; requires Traffic Manager or Front Door for cross-region routing.
pros: Integration with Front Door for global routing

cards.title: Storage Accounts
cards.description: Support RA-GRS and GRS for read access in the secondary region, but failover requires manual or automated promotion.
pros: Read access in secondary during primary outage
cons: Secondary region is read-only until failover

data.caption: Request flow across Azure regions with Traffic Manager and Front Door
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[User] --> B[Traffic Manager / Front Door]
    B -->|Primary Healthy| C[App Service East US]
    B -->|Primary Unhealthy| D[App Service West Europe]
    C --> E[SQL Database Primary]
    D --> F[SQL Database Secondary]
    E --> G[Geo-Replication]
    G --> F
    F -->|Failover| E

items: Verify the application resource group exists and is healthy in the failing region.
Check Azure Activity Log for deployment or provisioning failures in the secondary region.
Test the regional endpoint directly to distinguish routing issues from application failures.
Review Azure Front Door or Traffic Manager backend pool health probes and their responses.
Confirm the database failover group is configured and the secondary is readable.
Check for region-specific resource quotas that may block provisioning or scaling.

data.title: Regional quotas
data.text: Azure subscriptions have default quotas per region. A deployment that works in East US may fail in West Europe if the quota for App Service plans, cores, or storage accounts is exhausted. Request quota increases before you need them.

items: Redeploy the application to the secondary region if missing
Update Traffic Manager or Front Door backend pools to include the healthy endpoint
Verify health probes are configured correctly for the secondary endpoint
Enable auto-failover on Azure SQL or Cosmos DB if not already active
Test the failover in a controlled maintenance window
Monitor cross-region latency and set alerts for RTO breaches

items.question: Why does Azure Front Door show the backend as unhealthy in one region?
items.answer: Front Door health probes may fail if the application path is missing, TLS certificate is invalid, or the probe port is blocked by a firewall. Check the probe path and response code settings.

items.question: Is cross-region replication automatic for all Azure data services?
items.answer: No. Cosmos DB and Azure SQL require explicit configuration for geo-replication or failover groups. Storage accounts require RA-GRS or GRS to be enabled.

data.title: Fix a single-region Azure deployment
data.description: An e-commerce API is deployed only to East US. West Europe users experience 504 errors. Design the changes needed to serve West Europe from a local endpoint.
steps: Identify which Azure services need secondary region deployment
Choose between Traffic Manager and Front Door for global routing
Configure database geo-replication or failover groups
Update CI/CD to deploy to both regions
Test failover by disabling the primary region endpoint
data.expectedOutcome: A multi-region architecture that routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint and survives a single-region outage.

data.title: Summary
points: Azure resources are region-scoped unless configured for geo-replication
Use Traffic Manager or Front Door for global traffic routing
Enable database failover groups before you need them
Test regional failover regularly to validate RTO and RPO
Monitor quotas in every region where you deploy
data.takeaway: Multi-region resilience is an architecture decision, not an afterthought. Plan for regional failures before they occur.
